newsitem.title: UK: Long end attracts in U.S. and Germany.
newsitem.headline: Long end attracts in U.S. and Germany.

text.p: The long end of the yield curve for U.S. and German government bonds both offer appeal to investors despite contrasting economic backdrops, analysts said on Wednesday.
They said investors should not be deterred by below average cover for an auction of U.S. three-year Treasury-notes, but should look further along the yield curve.

"It's a replay of the November refunding where you had a fairly tepid three-year but reasonably good 10- and 30-year auctions," David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi International in London.

The U.S. quarterly refunding is the market focus this week. An auction of $17.75 billion of three-year notes was held on Tuesday, and issues for $12.0 billion of 10-year notes and $10.0 billion of 30-year bonds will follow on Wednesday and Thursday.
Hewitt said the 10- and 30-year sales were expected to go well despite any wariness following the three-year auction.
One reason for this was the small size of the new 10-year compared with $20 billion for the total of the old issue, thus increasing demand as people switch into the new bond, he said.

"That is partly reflected already in the fact that the roll is three basis points below. But even though the roll is quite wide, there will be reasonably good demand for the 10-year notes," said Hewitt.
The roll is the yield on the old bond minus the yield on the new bond.
The 30-year bond auction was also expected to go well.
"There has been a bit of steepening from 10s to 30s this year, so the very long end of the market is looking reasonably attractive," said Hewitt.
Analysts said the overall tone of the market was optimistic which would encourage investors to look for duration.

"The backdrop is quite favourable," said Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London. "The economic fundamentals, progress on the budget and lessened concern about a Fed rate hike are all favourable."
But she said there was no particular area of the curve which was likely to outshine any other.
"We are not anticipating a lot of movement over the next few quarters in terms of the shape of the curve," Gibbs said.
She said, barring a slight spike at the beginning of 1996, yields had been roughly at these levels since the second quarter of 1995, which fitted in with stable U.S. growth.
But Gibbs said the picture was different for Germany with the general market view being for a flattening of the German curve in the short term.

She said the 10-year Bund yield had been hovering around 5.50 percent in the belief that German investors would resist accepting anything lower, but that from a tactical, strategic and fundamental perspective such a move was valid.

"As people think more about a possible delay for EMU, funds are going into Germany, and in that context, from a tactical perspective any investors will be squeezed lower," she said. "They have good reason to call for lower German yields, So in terms of value we'd look to the long end of the German curve."
